I hate this slide every time it comes up, and now from CSAIL This has been false since before the slide was made. Automated systems make management decisions all the time (trading, logistics, customer service, insurance) & pretending they don't actually launders responsibility. An IBM slide from 1979.

It is especially rich coming from MIT and IBM, as both were the key to SAGE 20 years before this, an automated system that automatically assigned interceptors and missiles against incoming aircraft. Literally letting a computer make management decisions. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Automatic_Ground_Environment

Not an anti-MIT thing (I am an alumni) but it is a weird post since CSAIL faculty does tons of work on automated decision making. Better to emphasize all their work on ensuring accountability & alignment given that machines are, indeed, making more and more management decisions

Before you finalize your BFCM ad budget, sign up for your own email list. Then check what needs to change before your sale goes live. If your sale banner says 30% off, your popup offers 10%, and your welcome email sends 15%, shoppers shouldn’t have to guess which offer applies or whether they combine. You have time to catch that now. Here are four things I’d check: 1. Will your popup make sense alongside the sale? Plan your popup updates alongside your ads, site banners, and sale emails. If signing up will get shoppers an additional discount, explain how it works with the sale. Make the terms clear before they reach checkout. 2. What does signing up get them before BFCM? If you’re offering early access, be specific. “Get the Black Friday sale link 24 hours before everyone else” tells shoppers more than “Join our VIP list.” Your welcome email should confirm that promise and explain what happens next. 3. Will the entire welcome flow deliver the right offer? Review subject lines, body copy, and discount codes throughout the sequence. Updating the first email isn’t enough if email three still promotes an old offer. Also plan for someone who signs up before the sale but receives the next email after it starts. 4. Will the offer work on mobile? Once your sale setup is ready to test, follow the full path: submit the popup, open the email, tap the link, and add a product to your cart. Check minimum spend, exclusions, expiration dates, and the final price. Interesting finding about reasoning models and CoT. They find that reasoning models can control their chain of thought much better than earlier tests suggested. Earlier evaluations put the constraint in the user prompt and found very low controllability. Researchers put the same constraint inside the chain of thought as a self-instruction, and models followed it far more often. A generic reminder to follow the user's constraint also helped a lot. The self-instruction can be triggered from the user prompt alone, so no access to the reasoning channel is needed. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23257 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/reasoning-models-can-control-their-chains-of-thought-when-they-tell-themselves-t-2610.23257

Banger paper from Google DeepMind on open-ended math discovery with agents. This is one of the early, exciting works I have seen on autonomous AI-powered discoveries. (bookmark it) A Gemini-based agent found and formally verified new acceleration rules for eleven unresolved Turing machines in BB(6), the current frontier of the Busy Beaver problem. Busy Beaver is uncomputable, so no fixed list of problems exists. The agent has to pick machines, spot patterns in their execution traces, and propose compact rules that summarize many steps at once. Each proposed rule then goes through informal reasoning and a Lean proof. Only proved rules are kept, so the result does not depend on trusting the model's reasoning. The authors provisionally call these machines Cryptids. Their runs from a blank tape now have exact, compact descriptions, but whether they halt is still open. This is a good example of an agent producing new, formally checked mathematical results on problems it chose itself. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22603 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/at-the-limits-of-computability-steps-towards-autonomous-ai-discovery-on-the-busy-2610.22603

Recommended work from Meta on harnesses for proactive agents. The ProPerAgent harness raises accuracy from at most 15% with standard memory baselines to 38%, without changing the model's weights. But this success requires both a useful response and correct timing. The harness controls how personal memories reach the model as it observes the user's surroundings. First, the model identifies objects in view. A retrieval module uses those objects to search a graph of past experiences, preferences, and constraints. A separate LLM call then checks whether the retrieved memories justify offering help now. It filters out distracting or already resolved information and returns one concise piece of evidence, or nothing. The model uses that evidence and the current view to decide whether to speak or stay silent. That filtering step matters. Removing it drops accuracy from 37.3% to 24.0% in an ablation. Across the full harness, unnecessary interventions on clips that require silence fall to 15.3%, compared with 77.3% or 84.0% for standard RAG in the two evaluation modes. The harness also reaches 37.5% with Qwen3.8-27B without training. Additional RL training on that model raises accuracy to 42.4% by penalizing premature and repeated interventions. For proactive assistants, the harness needs to check whether a memory warrants an interruption before passing it to the model. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22671 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/properagent-toward-memory-driven-proactive-assistance-2610.22671
